summary: Comments on the file transfer proposal in RFC 114. The author thinks it is not strict enough about transactions: every message should get a reply and control should pass back and forth until the server ends the session. It also discusses error recovery during transfers.

eli5.summary: When you hand someone a heavy box, you wait for them to say got it. This note says the file helper should always answer, and explains what to do if the box gets dropped.

subtitle: A 1971 critique of the early file transfer proposal: answer every message, recover from errors in levels, and number the NCP.

tldr.problem: The file transfer proposal in RFC 114 did not say enough about how a transfer should be acknowledged, and early network software handled errors by closing the connection and starting over.
tldr.mechanism: The author asks that every transaction get a response, with the server always getting the last word, and proposes record access, a file directory request, multilevel error recovery and a version number for the NCP.
tldr.outcome: It is a set of suggestions that comment on and update RFC 114. It does not define a finished protocol.

facts.label: Key transaction codes
facts.value: R, S, L and new F (file directory)

today: RFC 133 is a 1971 set of comments that updates RFC 114, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes it. It records early ideas about acknowledgment, error recovery and NCP versioning rather than a finished standard.

sections.title: Handshaking in File Transfer
sections.content:
The author thinks the file transfer proposal in RFC 114 is not strict enough about what a transaction sequence is. Every transaction should prompt a response from its recipient, and control should pass back and forth until the server ends the exchange. The server always gets the last word.

The RFC gives sample exchanges. In a retrieval, the user sends an R request, the server answers rs (I have your file), the user says rr (send it), the server sends the first part, the user acknowledges with rr, and the server closes with + (all done). A store request runs the same way in the other direction.
sections.eli5: Every time you say something, the other side says something back, like a game of catch. The helper always makes the last throw.

sections.title: Extensions to the Protocol
sections.content:
The protocol needs a way to reach individual records of a file, which would matter once very large data bases appear on the network. The store (S) and retrieve (R) requests would accept a key made of a file name and a key name. A retrieve with a key returns the record after the matching key. A store with a key replaces that record, or appends it to the file if the key name does not exist. Each installation must supply the link between a key name and its record.

A lookup (L) request would list the key names in a file. A new transaction code F requests a file directory listing: the data field holds one or more path names, and the server returns a file listing every file that matches. A path name with no file name means all files on the given device.
sections.eli5: Instead of fetching a whole book, you could ask for one page by its label. You could also ask for a list of all the books on the shelf.

sections.title: Multilevel Error Recovery
sections.content:
The author notes that error recovery has been noticeably lacking: the usual approach is to close the connection and start from scratch. The proposal is a multilevel procedure.

If an error does not lose the third level transaction boundaries and affects only one side of a duplex connection, a transaction sequence abort is enough. In the sample, a data error is answered with an abort message, the server replies that it forgets the transfer, and the user asks again. A timeout is handled the same way. The server again has the last word. This works in any protocol that uses flagged blocking and duplex connections.

If that fails, the link must be cleared and resynchronized. The author suggests an 8-bit argument on the interrupt-on-link NCP messages (INR, INS): the receiver sends INR with an error code and discards incoming data, the sender flushes its queue, and the NCP sends INS with a new sync value. If all else fails, close the faulty socket.
sections.eli5: If a toy gets broken in the mail, first you ask for a new one. If the whole mailbox is a mess, you clear it out and begin again. Closing the mailbox is the last choice.

sections.title: NCP Version Numbers
sections.content:
The author suggests giving the NCP a version number. The next version would add two message types: WRU (who are you), which asks the receiving host for its version number, and IAM, which supplies it.

At first these would mean roughly can I talk to you, and over time they would come to mean what can you do. For that reason the version field should be large, with 32 bits suggested for expansion.
sections.eli5: Before talking, the computers could ask each other which edition of the rules they know, like checking you both have the same rulebook.

references.text: Bhushan, A., "A File Transfer Protocol", RFC 114, NIC 5823.
